title: VFR Cruising Altitudes, MEFs, and Glide Distance Planning

questions.text: Under 14 CFR 91.159, a pilot is flying with a magnetic COURSE of 282° at 6,000 feet MSL in level cruise flight more than 3,000 feet AGL. Is this altitude compliant, and what is the correct required altitude?

options.label: A
options.text: Non-compliant — a magnetic course of 282° falls in the Southwest quadrant (180°–359°), requiring an even-thousand plus 500-foot altitude; 6,000 feet MSL has no +500 suffix and violates 14 CFR 91.159

options.label: B
options.text: Compliant — 14 CFR 91.159 cruising altitude requirements apply only to IFR flights; VFR pilots may select any altitude above 3,000 AGL and are only required to comply with NEODD/SWEVEN below the flight level structure

options.label: C
options.text: Non-compliant — 14 CFR 91.159 requires all VFR cruising flights to fly at odd-thousand plus 500-foot altitudes regardless of magnetic course direction; even-thousand plus 500-foot altitudes are reserved for IFR aircraft

options.label: D
options.text: Compliant — a magnetic course of 282° falls in the Northeast quadrant (000°–179°) based on the compass bearing rounding convention, and odd-thousand altitudes (5,500 or 7,500) are legally incorrect for this course

questions.explanation: A magnetic course of 282° falls in the 180°–359° range — the Southwest quadrant under the NEODD/SWEVEN rule. Southwest = EVEN thousands + 500 feet. Legal altitudes include 4,500, 6,500, 8,500, 10,500, etc. Cruising at exactly 6,000 feet MSL is non-compliant — there is no +500 suffix. The +500 suffix is mandatory because it provides vertical separation from IFR aircraft cruising at the even thousands. The correct altitude for this course would be 6,500 feet MSL. Option B incorrectly maps 282° to the Northeast quadrant. Option C falsely exempts VFR pilots from 91.159. Option D inverts the odd/even assignment to quadrants.

questions.text: A pilot has a magnetic ground track (course) of 085° but due to a strong crosswind from the south, must fly a magnetic HEADING of 110° to maintain that track. Which VFR cruising altitude requirement applies under 14 CFR 91.159?

options.label: A
options.text: The heading of 110° determines the altitude rule — 110° falls in the Northeast quadrant (000°–179°), requiring an odd-thousand plus 500-foot altitude such as 5,500 or 7,500 feet MSL above 3,000 AGL

options.label: B
options.text: The average of the heading and course must be used — when wind correction angles exceed 10 degrees, the FAA requires pilots to average the magnetic heading and magnetic course to calculate the applicable cruising altitude under 91.159

options.label: C
options.text: The course of 085° determines the altitude rule — 085° falls in the Northeast quadrant (000°–179°), requiring an odd-thousand plus 500-foot altitude such as 3,500, 5,500, or 7,500 feet MSL above 3,000 AGL

options.label: D
options.text: Either the heading or course may be used — FAA AIM guidance states that pilots may elect to use whichever value is more convenient for altitude planning when heading and course diverge by more than 15 degrees due to wind

questions.explanation: 14 CFR 91.159 specifies that cruising altitudes are based on the MAGNETIC COURSE — the actual track over the ground — not the magnetic heading required to compensate for wind. The distinction is critical: heading is where the nose points to compensate for wind drift; course is the actual track over the earth's surface. In this scenario, the ground track (course) is 085° — Northeast quadrant = ODD + 500. The required altitude is 3,500, 5,500, 7,500, or 9,500 feet MSL depending on terrain. Option A incorrectly uses the magnetic heading to determine the altitude quadrant. Options C and D invent averaging methods that have no basis in 91.159 regulatory language.

questions.text: A sectional chart quadrant shows a Maximum Elevation Figure (MEF) of 3,700 feet. A pilot plans to cruise at 4,500 feet MSL on a legal SW-quadrant heading. What does the MEF value represent, and is 4,500 feet a safe cruising altitude for this quadrant?

options.label: A
options.text: The MEF represents the highest terrain or obstacle in the quadrant plus approximately 100 feet of buffer; 4,500 feet provides only 800 feet above the MEF, which does not meet the recommended 1,000-foot clearance minimum of 14 CFR 91.119 in non-congested areas

options.label: B
options.text: The MEF of 3,700 is derived by adding exactly 300 feet to the highest obstacle, so the actual highest terrain is 3,400 feet MSL; 4,500 feet provides 1,100 feet of clearance and meets 14 CFR 91.119 requirements comfortably

options.label: C
options.text: The MEF of 3,700 guarantees that no terrain or obstacle within the quadrant exceeds 3,700 feet MSL, making 4,500 feet MSL safe with 800 feet of obstacle clearance — adequate for VFR cruise under 14 CFR 91.119 in non-congested areas

options.label: D
options.text: The MEF is a minimum enroute altitude (MEA) equivalent for VFR aircraft; cruising above the MEF automatically satisfies all VFR altitude requirements under 14 CFR 91.159 and 91.119 without additional safety margin evaluation

questions.explanation: MEF (Maximum Elevation Figure) is calculated by taking the highest known terrain or man-made obstacle in the sectional quadrant and adding a buffer of approximately 100 feet (then rounding up to the next 100-foot value). The buffer is small — designed only to account for minor survey inaccuracies, not to provide operational safety margin. An MEF of 3,700 means the highest obstacle is approximately 3,600 feet. At 4,500 feet, the pilot has approximately 800 feet of clearance — below the 1,000-foot minimum recommended by 14 CFR 91.119 for non-congested areas. The operationally safe altitude would be 4,700 feet or higher (MEF + 1,000 feet), but 4,700 is not a legal cruising altitude for this SW-quadrant course — the next legal value above 4,700 would be 6,500 feet. Option C fabricates a 300-foot buffer. Option D mischaracterizes MEF as equivalent to an MEA and incorrectly claims regulatory compliance.

questions.text: A Cessna 172 pilot is cruising at 6,500 feet MSL, which is 5,000 feet AGL over forested terrain with no airports or suitable fields within 8 nautical miles. Using a best glide ratio of 10:1, approximately what is the maximum glide distance available, and can the pilot reach a suitable field?

options.label: A
options.text: Glide distance cannot be calculated from altitude alone — glide ratio varies with airspeed and wind; a calculation requires real-time wind data from the Winds Aloft forecast and a digital E6B before any engine-out planning conclusion can be made

options.label: B
options.text: Glide distance is approximately 50 nautical miles — the 10:1 ratio means for every 10 feet of altitude the plane travels 1 nautical mile, so 5,000 feet of altitude equals 500 nautical miles of glide range

options.label: C
options.text: Glide distance is approximately 5 nautical miles — insufficient to reach any suitable field 8 nm away; the pilot should immediately climb to a higher altitude to extend the engine-out footprint over this terrain

options.label: D
options.text: Glide distance is approximately 7.5 nautical miles — with 5,000 feet AGL at a 10:1 glide ratio, the pilot can cover approximately 50,000 feet forward, which converts to roughly 8.2 nautical miles — marginally reaching a field 8 nm away

questions.explanation: Glide distance calculation with a 10:1 ratio: the aircraft travels 10 feet horizontally for every 1 foot of altitude lost. At 5,000 feet AGL: 5,000 feet × 10 = 50,000 feet of horizontal distance. Converting: 50,000 ÷ 6,076 (feet per nautical mile) = approximately 8.2 nautical miles. This is marginally sufficient to reach a field 8 nm away — but only in no-wind, perfect-conditions glide to best glide speed. Any wind, incorrect speed, or obstacles reduces this margin significantly. The practical takeaway: the pilot is at the edge of the safety envelope over this terrain and should climb higher to provide meaningful glide distance margin over areas with no emergency landing sites. Option A underestimates the glide distance. Option C confuses the ratio — 10:1 means 10 feet horizontal per foot of altitude, not 1 nm per foot. Option D is excessive — basic glide distance planning uses still-air published Vg performance from the POH.

questions.text: A pilot planning a cross-country with a magnetic course of 090° must choose between cruising at 5,500 feet MSL or 7,500 feet MSL. The Winds Aloft forecast shows a 15-knot headwind at 6,000 feet and a 30-knot headwind at 9,000 feet. Terrain clears at 4,500 feet MSL with no landing hazards below. Which altitude better balances regulatory compliance, terrain clearance, and performance efficiency?

options.label: A
options.text: 7,500 feet — the 14 CFR 91.159 NEODD rule mandates that pilots must fly at the highest odd-thousand plus 500-foot altitude available for any NE magnetic course to maximize terrain clearance and emergency footprint simultaneously

options.label: B
options.text: 5,500 feet — both altitudes are legally compliant (NE course = odd + 500) and terrain-safe; the 15-knot headwind at 5,500 produces better groundspeed and fuel efficiency than the 30-knot headwind at 7,500, with no terrain clearance deficiency at either altitude

options.label: C
options.text: 7,500 feet — the NEODD rule requires a higher odd-thousand altitude for NE courses, and higher altitudes always provide better true airspeed, which compensates for the stronger headwind at higher altitude and ultimately produces better groundspeed

options.label: D
options.text: 5,500 feet — the NEODD rule only applies to flights above 9,000 feet MSL; any altitude between 3,000 AGL and 9,000 MSL is legally discretionary for VFR aircraft regardless of magnetic course direction

questions.explanation: Both 5,500 and 7,500 feet are legally valid for a NE magnetic course under 91.159 (odd + 500). Both provide adequate terrain clearance (MEF is below 4,500 feet MSL, so either altitude provides 1,000+ feet of clearance). The differentiating factor is performance: a 30-knot headwind at 7,500 vs. 15-knot headwind at 5,500 means the lower altitude produces better groundspeed, burns less fuel per nm traveled, and reduces total flight time. A higher TAS at altitude does not overcome a 15-knot additional headwind at most training aircraft cruise speeds. The intelligent DPE-satisfying answer demonstrates reasoned evaluation of winds vs. altitude — not a reflexive 'higher is always better.' Option A incorrectly claims higher altitude always beats headwind via TAS. Option C invents a 'highest possible' mandate in 91.159. Option D invents a 9,000 MSL threshold that does not exist.

questions.text: The 14 CFR 91.159 VFR cruising altitude requirement applies under which specific condition?

options.label: A
options.text: When operating above 18,000 feet MSL in Class A airspace, where all VFR traffic must apply the NEODD/SWEVEN rule to separate from IFR traffic on instrument approaches

options.label: B
options.text: Anytime a VFR aircraft is operated in controlled airspace at any altitude, including at pattern altitude in Class D airspace

options.label: C
options.text: Only during cross-country flights exceeding 50 nautical miles in Class E airspace; local area flights and flights in Class G airspace are exempt from the cruising altitude requirement

options.label: D
options.text: When operating more than 3,000 feet above the surface in level VFR cruise flight — the rule does not apply at or below 3,000 feet AGL or during climbs and descents

questions.explanation: 14 CFR 91.159 applies when a VFR aircraft is in level cruise flight more than 3,000 feet above the surface. The two important exclusions: (1) Below 3,000 feet AGL — no cruising altitude rule applies, which is why aircraft flying at pattern altitude (typically 800–1,000 AGL) or maneuvering below 3,000 AGL are not subject to 91.159. (2) During climbs and descents — 91.159 applies to level cruise, not transition altitudes. Option A extends the rule to any altitude including pattern altitude, which is incorrect. Option C invents a 50 nm cross-country threshold and Class G exemption — neither exists in 91.159. Option D inverts the rule (Class A is IFR-only; 18,000+ is Class A where VFR is prohibited).

questions.text: You are cruising at 5,500 feet MSL (approximately 2,000 feet AGL) over mountainous terrain. A MEF of 4,900 is shown on the sectional chart. You can see a suitable farm field about 5 miles to the south. Your engine quits unexpectedly. What is the SAFEST immediate action and assessment?

options.label: A
options.text: Maintain 5,500 feet as long as possible by pitching up to slow the descent before establishing best glide — stopping the altitude loss first gives maximum time to reach the farm field 5 miles south

options.label: B
options.text: Immediately pitch to best glide speed, assess glide distance available against the 5-mile field, and evaluate whether terrain between your position and the field allows a safe approach — if the glide math confirms you can reach the field, fly a controlled approach to it; if not, identify a closer alternative

options.label: C
options.text: Declare an emergency immediately and wait for ATC vectors to the nearest airport — ATC has radar and can guide you to the best possible landing site faster than any self-calculated glide ratio assessment under stress

options.label: D
options.text: Attempt an engine restart immediately at full throttle before starting any glide calculations — diagnosing and fixing the engine problem in the first 30 seconds is the priority before evaluating any forced landing options

questions.explanation: At 2,000 feet AGL with a 10:1 glide ratio, maximum glide distance is approximately 3.3 nautical miles (2,000 × 10 = 20,000 feet ÷ 6,076 = ~3.3 nm). The farm field is 5 miles away — outside the maximum glide range. The correct first action is pitching to best glide speed and scanning immediately for an achievable landing site within the actual 3–3.3 nm footprint. The farm field answer in a structured training scenario may still be evaluated — but the pilot must verify glide math before committing to it. Option A is Macho — pitching up above best glide dramatically degrades glide performance and may cause a stall; pitching up does not stop altitude loss, it just moves the stall point closer. Option C is Resignation — ATC cannot vector an engine-out aircraft in real time to a terrain alternate; the pilot must navigate this independently. Option D is Invulnerability — an engine restart attempt is appropriate but must be done WHILE maintaining best glide, not instead of glide planning.
questions.sjt_rationale: Option A is Macho — physically fighting the glide physics. Option C is Resignation — outsourcing a self-navigation problem to ATC. Option D is Invulnerability — overconfidence in restart success over glide planning. Option B maintains control, establishes performance, and evaluates survival options with accurate math.

questions.text: During checkride oral, the DPE asks: 'Why did you choose 5,500 instead of 9,500 for this cross-country? Higher is always safer.' What is the BEST response?

options.label: A
options.text: Maintain 5,500 without explanation — the DPE's statement is factually incorrect; higher is not always safer, and a pilot who lets a DPE's incorrect statement go unchallenged demonstrates cognitive compliance bias rather than aeronautical confidence

options.label: B
options.text: Ask the DPE to specify which regulation requires the highest available odd-thousand altitude for NE courses — placing the burden on the examiner to cite a regulation they cannot cite demonstrates regulatory knowledge and prevents the DPE from intimidating the applicant into an incorrect answer

options.label: C
options.text: Explain that 5,500 and 9,500 are both legally compliant for the NE magnetic course; the Winds Aloft forecast showed a 20-knot stronger headwind at 9,000 than at 6,000, making 5,500 more fuel-efficient; terrain clears at 4,200 MSL so both altitudes provide adequate terrain clearance; and 5,500 is sufficient for the engine-out glide footprint over the planned route's landing-site density

options.label: D
options.text: Agree with the DPE and change the altitude to 9,500 — the examiner has more experience and is pointing out a safety deficiency; accepting the correction demonstrates appropriate deference and situational humility

questions.explanation: The DPE's prompt 'higher is always safer' is a deliberate test — it is not always true, and a technically sound applicant knows this. The professional response is not to agree reflexively (Resignation) nor to challenge combatively (Macho), but to present the structured reasoning behind the altitude choice. A well-defended 5,500 choice that weighs winds, terrain, glide footprint, fuel, and regulatory compliance is exactly what the DPE is hoping to hear — it demonstrates that the applicant is a thinking pilot, not a rule-memorizer. Option A is Resignation — changing a defensible decision because of DPE pressure. Option C is technically correct in its reasoning but tactically wrong in delivery — refusing to explain is not a demonstration of knowledge. Option D is Macho — adversarially challenging the DPE rather than engaging collaboratively.
questions.sjt_rationale: Option A is Resignation — abandoning a defensible decision under social pressure. Option C is Macho-adjacent — stonewall defense rather than collaborative explanation. Option D is Macho — adversarial framing of a knowledge conversation. Option B is the mark of a pilot who reasoned, can explain, and will fly safely.
